claim: The intergenic IRES of Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV-IRES) forms a tight complex with 80S ribosomes capable of initiating the cell-free synthesis of complete proteins in the absence of initiation factors.
source: The intergenic IRES of Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV-IRES) forms a tight complex with 80S ribosomes capable of initiating the cell-free synthesis of complete proteins in the absence of initiation factors.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section (Jan et al. 2003; Pestova and Hillen, 2003).

claim: The first two cycles of elongation proceed much more slowly than subsequent cycles.
source: Our results demonstrate that 1) the first two cycles of elongation proceed much more slowly than subsequent cycles
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5, and Table 2, showing t1/2 values for different elongation steps.

claim: The reduced rates of the first two elongation cycles arise from slow pseudo-translocation and translocation steps.
source: 2) these reduced rates arise from slow pseudo-translocation and translocation steps
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Table 2 showing t1/2 values for Steps 3, 6, and 9 (translocation steps) are much longer than other steps.

claim: The retarding effect of ribosome-bound IRES on protein synthesis is largely overcome following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA.
source: 3) the retarding effect of ribosome-bound IRES on protein synthesis is largely overcome following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that translocation of tetrapeptidyl-tRNA (Step 12) is much faster than translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA (Step 9).

claim: The cap-dependent pathway involves recognition of 7-methyl-guanosine at the 5'-terminus of mRNA by a preinitiation complex of 40S ribosomal subunit and a host of initiation factors.
source: The cap-dependent pathway involves recognition of 7-methyl-guanosine at the 5'-terminus of mRNA by a preinitiation complex of 40S ribosomal subunit and a host of initiation factors prior to a scanning step that results in initiator aminoacyl-tRNA(aa-tRNA) pairing with a cognate start codon, followed by 60S binding to form the 80S initiator complex (Jackson et al., 2010; Aitken and Lorsch, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on eukaryotic translation initiation.

claim: The second pathway of eukaryotic protein synthesis initiation involves binding of the ribosome to an internal ribosome entry site (IRES).
source: The second pathway involves binding of the ribosome to an internal ribosome entry site (IRES), a structure that is present in many virus-encoded mRNAs, as well as in some cellular mRNAs (Fitzgerald and Semmler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on IRES-mediated translation.

claim: IRES structures are present in many virus-encoded mRNAs, as well as in some cellular mRNAs.
source: a structure that is present in many virus-encoded mRNAs, as well as in some cellular mRNAs (Fitzgerald and Semmler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on IRES distribution.

claim: Initiation of protein synthesis from an 80S·IRES complex can take place in the absence of some or even all of the initiation factors required in the cap-dependent pathway.
source: Initiation of protein synthesis from an 80S·IRES complex can take place in the absence of some or even all of the initiation factors required in the cap-dependent pathway (Filbin and Kieft, 2009), depending on the IRES source.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on IRES-mediated translation mechanisms.

claim: The intergenic IRES of Cricket Paralysis Virus forms a complex with 80S ribosomes that is capable of initiating the synthesis of complete proteins in cell-free assays completely lacking initiation factors.
source: The intergenic IRES of Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV-IRES) forms a complex with 80S ribosomes that is capable of initiating the synthesis of complete proteins in cell-free assays completely lacking initiation factors (Jan et al. 2003; Pestova and Hillen, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies demonstrating factor-independent translation.

claim: Prior to polypeptide chain initiation, the Dicistroviridae IRES structures from CrPV and Taura syndrome virus occupy all three tRNA binding sites (E, P, and A) on the ribosome.
source: More recently, high resolution structural studieshave shown that, prior to polypeptide chain initiation, the closely related Dicistroviridae IRES structures from CrPV (Fernandez et al., 2014; Muhs et al., 2015) and Taura syndrome virus (Koh et al., 2014) occupy all three tRNA binding sites (E, P, and A) on the ribosome, with the protein coding region beginning immediately downstream from IRES segment occupying the A-site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and reference to Figure 1 showing the IRES structure.

claim: The protein coding region begins immediately downstream from IRES segment occupying the A-site.
source: with the protein coding region beginning immediately downstream from IRES segment occupying the A-site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data cited and shown in Figure 1.

claim: CrPV-IRES binds with high affinity (Kd ~ 10 nM) to the 80S ribosome.
source: CrPV-IRES binds with high affinity (Kd ~ 10 nM) to the 80S ribosome (Jang and Jan, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study measuring binding affinity.

claim: Eukaryotic ribosomes used in the experiments are prepared from shrimp cysts.
source: In our experiments, eukaryotic ribosomes are prepared from shrimp cysts (Iwasaki and Kaziro, 1979)
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to the preparation method.

claim: Elongation factors are prepared from yeast.
source: elongation factors are prepared from yeast
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the source of elongation factors.

claim: Charged tRNAs are prepared from yeast and E. coli.
source: charged tRNAs are prepared from yeast and E. coli.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the source of tRNAs.

claim: The initial wt-codon triplet GCU encoding Ala has been replaced by UUC, encoding Phe, in the mutants used.
source: In addition, the peptide coding sequence attached to the 3'-end of the CrPV-IRES (Figure 1) has been mutated for ease in detection of peptide synthesis via 35S-Met incorporation. In all such mutants the initial wt-codon triplet GCU encoding Ala has been replaced by UUC, encoding Phe
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the mutations made to the IRES construct.

claim: The replacement of GCU with UUC has little effect on the expression of active luciferase in a cell-free protein synthesis assay.
source: a change that has little effect on the expression of active luciferase in a cell-free protein synthesis assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 comparing luciferase activity.

claim: In the absence of eEF2, the equilibrium position of Step 1 favors Structure 1 over Structure 2 by approximately 20-fold.
source: In the absence of eEF2 (blue trace), the equilibrium position of Step 1, a so-called pseudo-translocation step (Muhs et al., 2015) in which the IRES vacates the A-site, favors Structure 1 over Structure 2 by approximately 20-fold
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 3 and Table 1 showing rate constants that allow calculation of the equilibrium constant.

claim: The equilibrium between Structures 1 and 2 favoring Structure 1 over Structure 2 by approximately 20-fold is consistent with recent structural studies.
source: consistent with recent structural studies (Fernandez et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2014; Muhs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of the IRES-ribosome complex.

claim: Preincubation of 80S·IRES complex with 1 µM or 3 µM eEF2·GTP leads to clear biphasic binding of Phe-TC, with the more rapid and slower phases each accounting for ~50% of binding.
source: Preincubation of 80S·IRES complex with 1 µM or 3 µM eEF2·GTP leads to clear biphasic binding of Phe-TC, with the more rapid and slower phases each accounting for ~50% of binding, respectively (red and black traces).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The equilibrium between Structures 1 and 2 is shifted in the presence of eEF2·GTP, such that approximately half of 80S·IRES is present as Structure 2.
source: These results indicate that, consistent with recent results of Petrov et al. (2016), the equilibrium between Structures 1 and 2 is shifted in the presence of eEF2·GTP, such that approximately half of 80S·IRES is present as 2.
evidence: This is inferred from the biphasic kinetics observed in Figure 3 and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Added eEF2·GTP decreases all three apparent rate constants (k1, k-1, k2).
source: Although added eEF2·GTP decreases all three apparent rate constants, the effect is much greater on k-1 (~50-fold reduction) than on either k1 (~twofold reduction) or k2 (~fourfold reduction).
evidence: This is supported by the rate constants measured and presented in Table 1.

claim: The effect of eEF2·GTP is much greater on k-1 (~50-fold reduction) than on either k1 (~twofold reduction) or k2 (~fourfold reduction).
source: the effect is much greater on k-1 (~50-fold reduction) than on either k1 (~twofold reduction) or k2 (~fourfold reduction).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of rate constants in Table 1 with and without eEF2.

claim: The near identity of the red and black traces suggests that eEF2·GTP interacts with both Structures 1 and 2, with a dissociation constant significantly less than 1 µM.
source: The near identity of the red and black traces, performed at different eEF2·GTP concentrations, suggests that this factor interacts with both 1 and 2, with a dissociation constant significantly less than 1 µM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 1 µM and 3 µM eEF2·GTP give nearly identical kinetic traces in Figure 3.

claim: The large inhibitory effect of eEF2·GTP on k-1 is consistent with its role as a translocase.
source: The large inhibitory effect of eEF2·GTP on k-1 is consistent with its role as a translocase
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of eEF2 and the observed kinetic effect.

claim: A principal role of EF-G, the prokaryotic equivalent of eEF2, is to inhibit back-translocation.
source: and with recent results demonstrating that a principal role of EF-G, the prokaryotic equivalent of eEF2, is to inhibit back-translocation (Adio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on EF-G function.

claim: eEF2·GTP inhibition of k2 may be due, at least in part, to a requirement for eEF2·GDP dissociation prior to Phe-TC binding.
source: eEF2·GTP inhibition of k2 may be due, at least in part, to a requirement for eEF2·GDP dissociation prior to Phe-TC binding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed kinetic effect.

claim: Formation of Structure 4 from Structure 1 requires the presence of eEF2·GTP.
source: Formation of Structure 4 from Structure 1, as measured by the co-sedimentation assay, requires the presence of eEF2·GTP
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing that cosedimentation only occurs in the presence of eEF2·GTP.

claim: Formation of Structure 4 from Structure 1 proceeds at a considerably slower rate than formation of Structure 3 from Structure 1.
source: and proceeds at a considerably slower rate than formation of Structure 3 from Structure 1 (Figure 3)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of kinetic traces in Figure 3.

claim: The t1/2 for Step 3 (conversion of Structure 3 to Structure 4) is 210 ± 10 s.
source: allowing estimation of a t1/2 for Step 3, a second pseudo-translocation step involving conversion of 3 to 4, of 210 ± 10 s.
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic data in Figure 3 and reported in Table 2.

claim: Preincubation with eEF2·GTP (5' or 60') has no significant effect on the rate of formation of Structure 4 from Structure 1.
source: It is this further slow step that accounts for the lack of significant effect of preincubation with eEF2·GTP (5' or 60') on the rate of formation of 4 from 1 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing similar rates with different preincubation times.

claim: Reactions involving only TC binding and a single peptide bond formation (4 to 6; 7 to 9; 10 to 12) proceed in remarkably similar fashion, each showing biphasic behavior with a rapid phase accounting for 65 ± 10% of reaction proceeding with a t1/2 of ~6–9 s.
source: In all three cases, reactions involving only TC binding and a single peptide bond formation (4 to 6; 7 to 9; 10 to 12) proceed in remarkably similar fashion, each showing biphasic behavior with a rapid phase accounting for 65 ± 10% of reaction proceeding with a t1/2 of ~6–9 s
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: Reactions involving only TC binding and a single peptide bond formation show a slower, minor phase proceeding with t1/2 ~220–240 s, possibly corresponding to defective ribosomes.
source: and a slower, minor phase proceeding much more slowly (t1/2 ~220–240 s), possibly corresponding to defective ribosomes.
evidence: This is observed in the kinetic data in Figure 4, with speculation about the cause.

claim: Reactions involving formation of two peptide bonds (conversion of 4 to 9 or 7 to 12) are well approximated as single phase reactions with t1/2 values of 90–110 s.
source: Reactions involving formation of two peptide bonds, as in the conversion of 4 to 9 or 7 to 12 are well approximated as single phase reactions with t1/2 values of 90–110 s.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: The t1/2 value for translocation Step 6 is estimated as 84 s.
source: Conversion of 4 to 9 proceeds via Steps 4 – 8, allowing the t1/2 value for the translocation Step 6 to be estimated as 84 s, from the difference between the t1/2 value for the 4 to 9 reaction and the sum of the t1/2 values for the 4 to 6 and 7 to 9 reactions (major phases).
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: The t1/2 value for translocation Step 9 is estimated as 110 s.
source: Similarly, the t1/2 value for the translocation Step 9 can be estimated as 110 s from the difference between the t1/2 value for the 7 to 12 reaction and the sum of the t1/2 values for the 7 to 9 and 10 to 12 reactions.
evidence: This is calculated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: Translocation is the rate limiting step in each of the first two cycles of polypeptide elongation, proceeding from Structure 4 to Structure 10.
source: With this caveat, the results presented in Figure 4 lead to the clear conclusion that translocation is the rate limiting step in each of the first two cycles of polypeptide elongation, proceeding from 4 to 10.
evidence: This is concluded from the kinetic analysis of data in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: The [35S]-Met-TC cosedimentation rate with structure 7 outpaces the rate of peptide bond formation with Met-TC.
source: This strategy was successful for [35S]-Met–TC reaction with structure 7 (containing P-site bound PheLys-tRNALys, Figure 4C) or structure 10 (containing P-site bound PheValLys-tRNALys Figure 4D), in which the [35S]-Met-TC cosedimentation rates outpace the rates of peptide bond formation with Met-TC.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of kinetic traces in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The t1/2 value for TC binding Step 7 is 3 s.
source: These rate differentials permit estimates to be made for the t1/2 values of TC binding (Step 7, 3 s; Step 10, 2 s)
evidence: This is estimated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: The t1/2 value for TC binding Step 10 is 2 s.
source: These rate differentials permit estimates to be made for the t1/2 values of TC binding (Step 7, 3 s; Step 10, 2 s)
evidence: This is estimated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: The t1/2 value for peptide bond formation Step 8 is 4 s.
source: and peptide bond formation (Step 8, 4 s; Step 11, 7 s).
evidence: This is estimated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: The t1/2 value for peptide bond formation Step 11 is 7 s.
source: and peptide bond formation (Step 8, 4 s; Step 11, 7 s).
evidence: This is estimated from kinetic data in Figure 4 and reported in Table 2.

claim: Within Structures 8, 9, 11 and 12, Met-tRNAMet, PheLysMet-tRNAMet, and PheValLysMet-tRNAMet, when bound to the A-site, efficiently cosediment with ribosomes.
source: They also provide a clear indication that, within Structures 8, 9, 11 and 12, Met-tRNAMet, PheLysMet-tRNAMet, and PheValLysMet- tRNAMet, whenbound to the A-site, efficiently cosediment with ribosomes
evidence: This is supported by cosedimentation data in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Efficient cosedimentation of A-site bound tRNAs is typical for A-site bound tRNAs in conventional (non-IRES) elongation complexes.
source: which is typical for A-site bound tRNAs in conventional (non-IRES) elongation complexes (Warner and Rich, 1964; Nwagwu, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on tRNA binding in conventional elongation.

claim: For [35S]-Met–TC reaction with structure 4, the [35S]-Met-TC cosedimentation rate is much slower than the dipeptide formation rate.
source: However, for [35S]-Met–TC reaction with structure 4 (containing P-site bound Phe-tRNAPhe), the [35S]-Met-TC cosedimentation rate is much slower than the dipeptide formation rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of kinetic traces in Figure 4B.

claim: PheMet-tRNAMet, and possibly Met-tRNAMet as well, are not bound stably to the ribosome in Structures 5 and 6.
source: This indicates that PheMet-tRNAMet, and possibly Met-tRNAMet as well, are not bound stably to the ribosome in Structures 5 and 6
evidence: This is inferred from the slow cosedimentation rate compared to peptide formation rate in Figure 4B.

claim: Only PheMet-tRNAMet bound to the P-site (Structure 7) is fully recovered by cosedimentation.
source: and that only PheMet-tRNAMet bound to the P-site (Structure 7) is fully recovered by cosedimentation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cosedimentation kinetics in Figure 4B.

claim: The lability of the A-site tRNAs in structures 5 and 6 may be due to IRES binding to the E-site.
source: It is possible that the lability of the A-site tRNAs in structures 5 and 6 is due to IRES binding to the E-site, which is absent in structures 8, 9 and 11, 12, and may reflect an allosteric A-site: E-site interaction.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lability.

claim: Evidence for allosteric A-site/E-site interactions has been presented for both bacterial and eukaryotic ribosomes.
source: Evidence for allosteric A-site/E-site interactions has been presented for both bacterial and eukaryotic ribosomes (Nierhaus 1990; Chen et al., 2011; Ferguson et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on ribosome allostery.

claim: The general validity of allosteric A-site/E-site interaction has been questioned.
source: although the general validity of this interaction has been questioned (Semenkov et al., 1996; Petropoulos and Green, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature questioning the allosteric interaction.

claim: Puromycin (1 mM) reacts with A-site bound PheValLys-tRNALys about 20 times more slowly (t1/2 1400 ± 300 s) than it reacts with P-site bound PheValLys-tRNALys (t1/2 76 ± 16 s).
source: As shown in Figure 5A, puromycin (1 mM) reacts with A-site bound PheValLys-tRNALys, Structure 9, about 20times more slowly (t1/2 1400 ± 300 s) than it reacts with P-site bound PheValLys-tRNALys(t1/2 76 ± 16 s).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 5A.

claim: The t1/2 value for puromycin reaction with PheValLys-tRNALys undergoing translocation from the A- to P-site is 170 ± 30 s.
source: The corresponding t1/2 value for puromycin reaction with PheValLys-tRNALys undergoing translocation from the A- to P-site is 170 ± 30 s.
evidence: This is measured from kinetic data in Figure 5A.

claim: The increase of approximately 100 s for translocating PheValLys-tRNALys vs. translocated PheValLys-tRNALys closely matches the t1/2 value of 110 ± 30 s estimated for the translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA.
source: This increase of approximately 100 s for translocating PheValLys-tRNALysvs. translocated PheValLys-tRNALys closely matches the t1/2 value of 110 ± 30 s estimated above for the translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA (Table 2) and can be assigned to the translocating step.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of kinetic data from Figure 5A and Table 2.

claim: The rates of puromycin reaction with translocating and translocated PheValLysMet-tRNAMet are indistinguishable from one another (t1/2 values of 37 ± 4 s and 46 ± 7 s, respectively).
source: In contrast, the rates of puromycin reaction with translocating and translocated PheValLysMet-tRNAMet (Structure 13)are indistinguishable from one another (t1/2 values of 37 ± 4 s and 46 ± 7 s, respectively, Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 5B.

claim: Translocation of PheValLysMet-tRNAMet proceeds rapidly with respect to puromycin reaction.
source: a clear demonstration that translocation of PheValLysMet-tRNAMet proceeds rapidly with respect to puromycin reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the indistinguishable rates of puromycin reaction with translocating and translocated PheValLysMet-tRNAMet in Figure 5B.

claim: The upper limit value of t1/2 for the translocation Step 12 is ≤10 s.
source: Our results allow us to estimate an upper limit value of t1/2 for the translocation Step 12 of ≤10 s.
evidence: This is estimated from the puromycin reactivity data in Figure 5B and reported in Table 2.

claim: Puromycin reacts at similar rates with translocated PheValLys-tRNALys (Structure 10, t1/2 76 ± 16 s) and PheValLysMet-tRNAMet (Structure 13, t1/2 46 ± 7 s).
source: Puromycin reacts at similar rates with translocated PheValLys-tRNALys (Structure 10, t1/2 76 ± 16 s) and PheValLysMet-tRNAMet (Structure 13, t1/2 46 ± 7 s).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The puromycin reaction rates with eukaryotic P-site bound peptidyl-tRNA are consistent with those reported by others for eukaryotic P-site bound Met-tRNAMet, N-AcPhe-tRNAPhe, and Cy3-Met-tRNAMet.
source: These rates, while consistent with those reported by others for puromycin reaction with eukaryotic P-site bound Met-tRNAMet (Lorsch and Herschlag, 1999), N-AcPhe-tRNAPhe (Ioannou et al., 1997), and Cy3-Met-tRNAMet (Ferguson et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature on puromycin reactivity.

claim: The puromycin reaction rates with eukaryotic P-site bound peptidyl-tRNA are several hundred-fold slower than those measured for puromycin reaction with prokaryotic P-site bound peptidyl- or fMet-tRNA.
source: are several hundred-fold slower than those measured for puromycin reaction with prokaryotic P-site bound peptidyl- or fMet-tRNA.
evidence: This is a comparison with known rates from prokaryotic systems.

claim: The slow puromycin reactivity of eukaryotic P-site bound peptidyl-tRNA largely explains why the rate reduction for puromycin reaction with A-site vs. P-site bound peptidyl-tRNA is so much more modest for eukaryotic ribosomes (~20-fold) than for prokaryotic ribosomes (103–104-fold).
source: This largely explains why the rate reduction for puromycin reaction with A-site vs. P-site bound peptidyl-tRNA is so much more modest for eukaryotic ribosomes (~20-fold, Figure 5A) than for prokaryotic ribosomes (103–104-fold, Pan et al., 2007; Semenkov et al., 1992 ; Sharma et al., 2004; Peske et al., 2004 ).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of data in Figure 5A with cited literature on prokaryotic ribosomes.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, aa-tRNA binding and peptide bond formation proceed with an overall t1/2 of 6 – 9 s for each of the three elongation steps studied.
source: Above we have demonstrated that, under our conditions, aa-tRNA binding and peptide bond formation proceed with an overall t1/2of 6 – 9 s for each of the three elongation steps we have studied.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: Synthesis of a longer peptide that required the tripeptidyl-tRNA translocation step (Step 9) would proceed significantly more slowly than synthesis not requiring this step.
source: This relative constancy, coupled with the much slower translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA (Step 9) vs. tetrapeptidyl-tRNA (Step 12), leads to the prediction that synthesis of a longer peptide that required the tripeptidyl-tRNA translocation step (Step 9) would proceed significantly more slowly than synthesis not requiring this step.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the kinetic data in Figures 4 and 5 and Table 2.

claim: Octapeptide FKVRQWLM formation is much slower when synthesis is initiated with P-site bound PheLys-tRNALys (Structure 7) vs. P-site bound PheLysVal-tRNAVal (Structure 10).
source: In the second approach we verified this prediction by demonstrating that octapeptide FKVRQWLM formation, as measured by the cosedimentation assay, is much slower when synthesis is initiated with P-site bound PheLys-tRNALys (Structure 7) vs. P-site bound PheLysVal-tRNAVal (Structure 10) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 5C.

claim: The rates of FKVRQWLM synthesis are only marginally increased when reaction is initiated with P-site bound tetrapeptidyl-tRNA or pentapeptidyl-tRNA as compared with tripeptidyl-tRNA.
source: Indeed, the rates of FKVRQWLM synthesis are only marginally increased when reaction is initiated with P-site bound tetrapeptidyl-tRNA or pentapeptidyl-tRNA as compared with tripeptidyl-tRNA
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 5C.

claim: The retarding effect of ribosome-bound IRES on protein synthesis is largely overcome following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA.
source: reinforcing the notion that the retarding effect of ribosome-bound IRES on protein synthesis is largely overcome following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the kinetic data in Figure 5C showing similar rates for synthesis starting from different peptidyl-tRNAs.

claim: Translocation during the first elongation cycle (Step 6) clearly requires displacement of the IRES from the E-site.
source: Translocation during the first elongation cycle (Step 6) clearly requires displacement of the IRES from the E-site, so it is not unexpected that it would be slow.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement shown in Figure 1 and the kinetic data.

claim: The slow rate of Step 9 might be due to a full dissociation of IRES from the ribosome during this step.
source: The slow rate of Step 9 might be due to a full dissociation of IRES from the ribosome during this step, a suggestion that could be tested by appropriately designed structural studies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed slow translocation rate.

claim: Following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA from the A- to P-site, the pace of nascent peptide chain elongation picks up dramatically.
source: In any case, our results do clearly demonstrate that, following translocation of tripeptidyl-tRNA from the A- to P-site, the pace of nascent peptide chain elongation picks up dramatically.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data in Figure 5 showing much faster translocation of tetrapeptidyl-tRNA compared to tripeptidyl-tRNA.

claim: Prior results have shown that initial aa-tRNA binding to an 80S·IRES complex requires eEF2·GTP.
source: Prior results have shown that initial aa-tRNA binding, in the form of a ternary complex, to an 80S·IRES complex, as measured either by cosedimentation (Fernandez et al., 2014), or by filter binding and toeprinting (Yamamoto et al., 2007), requires eEF2·GTP
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: The conclusion that initial aa-tRNA binding can only bind to the 80S·IRES complex after an eEF2-dependent translocation event is incorrect.
source: leading to the conclusion that initial aa-tRNA binding can only bind to the 80S·IRES complex after an eEF2-dependent translocation event (Fernandez et al., 2014). While we agree with the experimental results, and have in fact reproduced the cosedimentation result in our own work, we disagree with the conclusion.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their own experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Ternary complex binding measured in situ, which can monitor labile binding to the A-site (Structure 3), does not require eEF2·GTP.
source: This is because these earlier experiments only measured stable aa-tRNA binding, corresponding to formation of Structure 4 in which aa-tRNA binds to the P-site. However, it is clear from the anisotropy experiment conducted in the absence of added eEF2·GTP (Figure 3, blue trace) that ternary complex binding measured in situ, which can monitor labile binding to the A-site (Structure 3)does not require eEF2·GTP.
evidence: This is supported by the anisotropy data in Figure 3 showing binding in the absence of eEF2.

claim: The equilibrium between Structure 1 (closed A-site) and Structure 2 (open A-site), which strongly favors Structure 1, is pulled to the right by aa-tRNA binding.
source: This is easily understood as an example of Le Chaltelier's principle, in which the equilibrium between Structure 1 (closed A- site)and Structure 2 (open A- site), which strongly favors Structure 1, is pulled to the right by aa-tRNA binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on chemical equilibrium principles and the observed kinetics.

claim: Preincubation with eEF2 shifts the equilibrium between Structures 1 and 2 to the right, leading to an initial rapid phase of reaction with Phe-TC.
source: Preincubation with eEF2 also shifts the equilibrium to the right, leading to an initial rapid phase of reaction with Phe-TC (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the biphasic kinetics observed in Figure 3 with eEF2 preincubation.

claim: Earlier toeprinting results showed no shift in IRES position within the 80S·CrPV-IRES complex on addition of eEF2 alone.
source: This latter shift, for which the results presented in Figure 3 provide strong inferential evidence, appears to be at odds with earlier toeprinting results showing no shift in IRES position within the 80S·CrPV-IRES complex on addition of eEF2 alone (Pestova et al., 2003; Jan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior toeprinting studies.

claim: The apparent inconsistency between the current results and earlier toeprinting results likely arises from eEF2 dissociation from the ribosome during the toeprinting assay.
source: In agreement with the suggestion of Muhs et al. (2015), we believe it likely that this apparent inconsistency arises from eEF2 dissociation from the ribosome during the toeprinting assay (Pestova et al., 1996), with the consequent favoring of Structure 1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation and reasoning about the toeprinting assay conditions.

claim: GTP is required for tight binding of eEF2 to the ribosome.
source: This is because GTP is required for tight binding of eEF2 to the ribosome (Nygård and Nilsson, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on eEF2 binding.

claim: The toeprinting assay is carried out for an extended period of time (45 min) under non-denaturing conditions in the absence of added GTP.
source: but the toeprinting assay is carried out for an extended period of time (45 min) under non-denaturing conditions in the absence of added GTP
evidence: This is a description of the toeprinting assay conditions from cited literature.

claim: The toeprinting assay conditions would eventually deplete GTP due to ribosome-dependent eEF2·GTP hydrolysis.
source: conditions that would eventually deplete GTP due to ribosome-dependent eEF2·GTP hydrolysis (Nygård and Nilsson, 1989).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known GTPase activity of eEF2 and the assay conditions.

claim: The toeprinting assay is performed at a Mg2+ concentration of 10.5 mM, considerably higher than the 5 mM used in the kinetic studies.
source: In addition, the toeprinting assay is performed at a Mg2+ concentration of 10.5 mM, considerably higher than the 5 mM used in our kinetic studies, which could also affect the 1 to 2 equilibrium position.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental conditions that could affect the results.

claim: The in vitro system used is quite heterogeneous, with ribosomes derived from shrimp cysts, yeast elongation factors, and yeast and E. coli charged tRNAs.
source: First, our in vitro systemis quite heterogeneous, with ribosomes derived from shrimp cysts, yeast elongation factors, and yeast and E. coli charged tRNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system used.

claim: IRESs can initiate translation on ribosomes from many eukaryotic organisms, including shrimp.
source: However, as reviewed in Koh et al. (2014), IRESs can initiate translation on ribosomes from many eukaryotic organisms, including shrimp (Cevallos and Sarnow, 2005), indicating that the molecular mechanism is not species-specific.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on IRES function across species.

claim: CrPV IRESs can initiate translation on ribosomes from yeast to human.
source: CrPV IRESs in particular can initiate translation on ribosomes from yeast (Thompson et al., 2001) to human (Spahn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating CrPV IRES function in different organisms.

claim: Eukaryotic elongation factors have structures that are very strongly conserved.
source: Furthermore, eukaryotic elongation factors have structures that are very strongly conserved (Soares et al., 2009; Jørgensen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of elongation factors.

claim: There is strong evidence that charged tRNAs from one species form functional complexes with both eEF1A and ribosomes from a different species.
source: and there is strong evidence that charged tRNAs from one species form functional complexes with both eEF1A and ribosomes from a different species (Jackson et al., 2001; Ferguson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cross-species tRNA function.

claim: Mutations in the downstream sequence are, in general, tolerated without substantial effect on initiation of translation.
source: This is also unlikely to pose a major difficulty, given the strong evidence that mutations in the downstream sequence are, in general, tolerated without substantial effect on initiation of translation (Tsukiyama-Kohara et al., 1992; Wang et al., 1993; Hellen and Sarnow, 2001; Rijnbrand et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the effects of downstream sequence mutations.

claim: Mutations of some downstream sequences do give rise to relatively minor changes in IRES activity.
source: although mutations of some downstream sequences do give rise to relatively minor changes in IRES activity (Kim et al., 2003; Shibuya et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing minor effects of certain mutations.

claim: The elongation rate of even the later cycles of IRES-dependent elongation is quite slow (~0.1 s-1).
source: Third, the elongation rate of even the later cycles of IRES-dependent elongation (Figure 5C) is quite slow (~0.1 s-1).
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic data in Figure 5C.

claim: The elongation rate of ~0.1 s-1 is essentially identical to that reported for tripeptide synthesis in a cap-dependent yeast-based in vitro translation system.
source: Although this rate is essentially identical to that reported for tripeptide synthesis in a cap-dependent yeast-based in vitro translation system which requires five initiation factors and eEF3 in addition to eEF1A and eEF2 (Acker et al., 2007; Eyler and Green, 2011; Gutierrez et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies measuring elongation rates in cap-dependent systems.

claim: The elongation rate of ~0.1 s-1 is 1.5–2 orders of magnitude slower than rates of peptide elongation estimated for intact eukaryotic cells at 37°C (3–10 s-1).
source: it is 1.5–2 orders of magnitude slowerthan rates of peptide elongation that have been estimated for intact eukaryotic cells at 37°C (3–10 s-1) (Boehlke and Friesen, 1975; Hershey, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies measuring elongation rates in intact cells.

claim: In many eukaryotic cells, the protein synthesis machinery is highly organized, containing several components, including ribosomes, a multi-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex, eEF-1A, and several auxiliary proteins.
source: There is evidence that, in many eukaryotic cells, the protein synthesis machinery is highly organized, containing several components, including ribosomes, a multi-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex, eEF-1A, and several auxiliary proteins (Negrutskii et al., 1994; Negrutskii and El'skaya, 1998; David et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the organization of the translation machinery.

claim: The organized structure of the protein synthesis machinery optimizes translation rate by coordinating synthetase activities to facilitate channeling of aa-tRNAs to the elongating ribosomes.
source: It has been suggested that this organized structure optimizes translation rate by coordinating synthetase activities to facilitate channeling of aa-tRNAs to the elongating ribosomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature about the function of the organized translation machinery.

claim: Protein synthesis in a permeabilized mammalian cell proceeds 40-fold faster than what is obtained in a cell-free system prepared from the same cells.
source: Thus, protein synthesis in a permeabilized mammalian cell, in which this structure is likely to be preserved, proceeds 40-fold faster than what is obtained in a cell-free system prepared from the same cells which presumably lacks this structure (Negrutskii et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study comparing translation rates in different systems.

claim: The slow rates measured for both the IRES-dependent and cap-dependent in vitro systems could be due, at least in part, to their lack of aa-tRNA channeling.
source: The slow rates measured for both the IRES-dependent and cap-dependent in vitro systems could be due, at least in part, to their lack of aa-tRNA channeling.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed slow rates.

claim: aa-tRNA channeling would be unlikely to accelerate the very slow translocation rates in the initial peptide elongation cycles.
source: Such channeling would be unlikely to accelerate the very slow translocation rates in the initial peptide elongation cycles reported in this work, although we cannot exclude the possibility that other proteins present in vivo might have such effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of translocation and the nature of aa-tRNA channeling.

claim: It is generally assumed that eEF2 functions in catalyzing eukaryotic elongation in much the same way that EF-G catalyzes prokaryotic elongation.
source: As one example, it is generally assumed, based on extensive structural similarities (Jørgensen et al., 2006), that eEF2 functions in catalyzing eukaryotic elongation in much the same way that EF-G catalyzes prokaryotic elongation
evidence: This is a statement about a common assumption in the field, supported by citation.

claim: eEF2 is subject to post-translational modifications not found in EF-G, with clear consequences for activity but little understanding of mechanism.
source: but this assumption does not take into account some important structural differences, including the fact that eEF2 is subject to post-translational modifications not found in EF-G, with clear consequences for activity but, as yet, little understanding of mechanism (Dever and Green, 2012; Mittal et al., 2013 ; Greganova et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on eEF2 post-translational modifications.

claim: The CrPV-IRES based system should permit detailed rate and structural dynamic studies of eEF2 catalytic function.
source: The CrPV-IRES based system should permit detailed rate and structural dynamic studies of eEF2 catalytic function, of the kind that have proved so useful in elucidating EF-G function in bacterial protein synthesis (Pan et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Salsi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prospective statement about the utility of the system, supported by citations to analogous studies in prokaryotic systems.
